title: Which emergency service should I use? (Royal Surrey)
intro: Royal Surrey's Emergency Department is at the Royal Surrey County Hospital in Guildford. For a minor injury or illness, the Urgent Treatment Centre at Haslemere Hospital is often quicker.

sections.heading: Life-threatening emergency
points: Call 999 now for: signs of a heart attack or stroke, severe breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding that will not stop, seizures (fits), or loss of consciousness.
The hospital's own words: "If you have a life-threatening illness or injury then you should dial 999."

sections.heading: Emergency Department — Royal Surrey County Hospital, Guildford
points: Egerton Road, Guildford GU2 7XX. Main switchboard 01483 571 122.
Patients are seen in order of clinical priority, so if your problem is less urgent you may face a very long wait.
If your condition is not life-threatening, contact NHS 111 first — NHS 111 can book you in to be seen quickly and safely.
If you arrive without being referred by NHS 111 or a GP, you will be asked triage questions and a streaming nurse may book you into a GP, the Urgent Treatment Centre, a dentist or a pharmacy instead.

sections.heading: Urgent Treatment Centre — Haslemere Hospital
points: Church Lane, Haslemere GU27 2BJ. Phone 01483 956 524.
Open daily 8am to 5pm; the last new patient booking is at 4pm. Walk in, or call NHS 111 for a time slot.
For adults and children over one year old. Run by emergency nurse and paramedic practitioners and doctors, with X-ray on site.

Treats injuries and illnesses from the last two weeks: strains and sprains, suspected broken limbs, minor head injuries, minor scalds and burns, skin infections and rashes, eye problems, feverish illness in adults and children, abdominal pain, emergency contraception.

Cannot treat: serious or life-threatening problems, injuries or conditions lasting more than two weeks, head injuries or falls with any loss of consciousness, toothache, mental health problems, pregnancy-related problems, vomiting and diarrhoea, overdoses or alcohol-related problems, children under one.
Good to know: the hospital's Emergency Department page gives the centre's hours as Monday to Friday, while the centre's own page says daily. Before travelling at a weekend, ring 01483 956 524.
sections.warning: The Urgent Treatment Centre is not a 24-hour service. Outside 8am to 5pm, call NHS 111 — or 999 if it could be serious.

sections.heading: Not sure where to go?
points: Use NHS 111 — call 111 or go to 111.nhs.uk — day or night.

title: Urgent eye problems (Royal Surrey)
intro: Royal Surrey's Ophthalmology department runs an Eye Emergency clinic. Phone the eye nurses first so they can tell you whether and when to come.

sections.heading: Go straight to A&E now if you have
points: A chemical splash or chemical injury to the eye.
A penetrating injury, or any significant trauma to the eye.
A foreign body stuck in the eye.
Eye pain together with headache, nausea or vomiting and a sudden deterioration in your vision.

sections.heading: Eye Emergency clinic — Royal Surrey County Hospital
points: Call the eye nurses on 01483 571 122, extension 4648, if you need to be seen in the Eye Emergency clinic.
Ophthalmology opening hours: Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm.
Level B, West Wing, Outpatients Department 10. Eye reception is extension 2567.

sections.heading: Out of hours
points: The hospital's page lists no out-of-hours eye number. Outside Monday to Friday 8am to 6pm, call NHS 111 — or 999, or go to the Emergency Department, for a serious eye injury or sudden loss of vision.
Minor eye injuries can also be seen at the Haslemere Urgent Treatment Centre, open daily 8am to 5pm (01483 956 524).

sections.heading: See an optician or GP the same day for
points: A red or sticky eye without pain or change in vision.
A gradual change in your vision.
Dry, itchy or watery eyes.

title: Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS) — Royal Surrey
intro: PALS is the hospital's team for advice, concerns and help sorting out problems while you are a patient. It is free and confidential.

sections.heading: How PALS can help
points: Answer questions about your care and help you understand what is happening.
Raise a concern quickly and informally with the right team.
Explain how to make a formal complaint if you want to.

sections.heading: Contact PALS (Royal Surrey)
points: Phone 01483 402757 — Monday to Friday, 9am to 3pm (except bank holidays).
The PALS office is at Royal Surrey County Hospital, Egerton Road, Guildford GU2 7XX.
If you need urgent advice outside PALS opening times, the hospital says to contact the main switchboard, 01483 571 122, and ask to speak to the site manager.

title: Urgent dental problems (Royal Surrey area)
intro: A&E cannot usually treat dental problems. The NHS urgent dental route is via your own dentist or NHS 111 — this page explains how it works and when A&E is the right place.

sections.heading: Get an urgent dental appointment
points: If you have a dentist, call them first and ask for an urgent appointment.
If you don't have a dentist, or they're closed: call 111 or use 111.nhs.uk — NHS 111 arranges urgent dental care in the Royal Surrey area.
You should be offered urgent dental treatment within 24 hours or 7 days, depending on your symptoms.
A knocked-out adult tooth needs emergency dental care within 1 hour, or as soon as possible — keep the tooth in milk and go straight via 111.

sections.heading: Go to A&E (not a dentist) if you have
points: Serious injuries to your face or jaw.
Heavy bleeding from your mouth that will not stop.
Severe swelling of your mouth, lips, throat or neck, with difficulty breathing or swallowing.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: Your GP cannot provide dental treatment — 111 is the right route.
Most adults need to pay the NHS charge for dental appointments, including urgent ones.

title: Fracture clinic — what happens after the Emergency Department (Royal Surrey)
intro: At Royal Surrey, follow-up after many fractures and other injuries is by the physiotherapy fracture clinic, which starts with a phone call.

sections.heading: Your referral
points: Only the Emergency Department can refer you to this service — your GP or the Urgent Treatment Centre cannot.
A chartered physiotherapist will call you within two weeks of your injury, at an arranged time, to discuss your injury and give personalised advice and exercises.
Clinics are virtual or by telephone. If you need one, the physiotherapist books a face-to-face appointment during the call.

sections.heading: Go back to the Emergency Department if
points: Your pain is getting worse rather than better, or is not controlled by the painkillers you were given.
Your fingers or toes become numb, tingly, very swollen, cold, pale or blue.
Your plaster cast or splint feels too tight, cracks, becomes loose, or gets wet and soft.
sections.warning: These can be signs of pressure on nerves or blood vessels — do not wait for the phone call.

sections.heading: Good to know
points: Keep the injured limb raised above the level of your heart when you can, especially in the first few days.
If you have not heard from the physiotherapy team two weeks after your injury, ring 01483 464 153.
